newsitem.title: USA: Thanks to El Nino, Atlantic hurricane forecast cut.
newsitem.headline: Thanks to El Nino, Atlantic hurricane forecast cut.

text.p: The warm water current known as El Nio should provide relief to tropical areas most vulnerable to hurricanes during the 1997 Atlantic season, although it could make things worse for areas further north, a noted forecaster said on Wednesday.

Prof. William Gray of Colorado State University, who issues hurricane forecasts four times a year, updated his outlook for the current Atlantic hurricane season to predict 11 tropical storms, of which he expected six to become hurricanes and two of those intense hurricanes.
The updated forecast -- Gray's last came on June 6 -- reduced by one Gray's expectations for hurricanes and intense hurricanes during the six-month June 1-Nov. 30 season.

"We've got a group of very mixed global climatic signals, which makes it a very difficult year," Gray said. "We're still going for a much stronger hurricane year than should occur during a typical El Nio year because many favorable factors for hurricane activity are present in the Atlantic Basin."
If Gray's forecast proves accurate, 1997 would be an above-average year for named storms and hurricanes, although below average for killer, intense hurricanes of Category 3 or higher.
In an average year the Atlantic season offers 9.3 tropical storms, 5.8 hurricanes and 2.2 intense, or major, hurricanes, with maximum sustained winds of 111 mph (179 kph) or more.
If Gray is on target, the three-year period stretching from 1995-1997 would be the most active three years for hurricane activity ever recorded. There were 13 named storms in 1996 and 19 in 1995.
Gray's hurricane forecasts do not predict how many storms might make landfall or where they might hit.
Tropical depressions become tropical storms and are given names when maximum sustained winds hit 39 mph (63 kph). Tropical storms become hurricanes when such winds reach 74 mph (119 kph).

In making forecasts, Gray's researchers analyze a range of global weather indicators such as sea surface temperatures in the Atlantic, rainfall in the Sahel region of West Africa where tropical systems often form, and high-level winds.
He said the El Nio forming in the Pacific this year turned out to be much stronger than he expected when he released the June forecast.
The El Nio, a period of warmer-than-normal water temperatures that causes world climatic chaos, can alleviate Atlantic hurricane misery.
The higher water temperatures tend to cause strong winds to blow in a westerly direction from the Pacific to the Atlantic, typically disrupting developing hurricanes.

But Gray said the winds produced by the weather phenomenon this year also might help shift hurricane formation from tropical Africa to the Atlantic Basin, which could put some storms at higher latitudes, closer to the United States.
